title: Coming from Windows
markdown:
# Coming from Windows

SP+ may look unfamiliar after Windows, but it is still a work computer: open an app, work in a window, save a file, and close it when you are done. You do not need to learn a new profession to get your work done.

## The Windows names you already know

A few names change. The job does not.

| In Windows | On SP+ | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Start menu | Applications menu | Finding and opening an app |
| File Explorer | **Dolphin**, the Files app | Seeing folders and opening files |
| Settings or Control Panel | **System Settings** | Changing a computer setting |
| Windows installer | **Fin** | Checking whether software is needed and adding it safely |

If you cannot see the equivalent of a Windows control, do not hunt through unfamiliar menus. Ask Fin what it is called here.

## The three things that feel different first

**Files have a different app name.** Open **Dolphin** when you want the same job as File Explorer. Your folders and documents are still yours. It does the same basic job.

**Settings are in one place.** Open **System Settings** for computer choices rather than looking for Control Panel. This is where a setting belongs when it affects the computer rather than one particular app.

**Software does not arrive as an `.exe` file.** A Windows download ending in `.exe` is not the safe installation route on SP+. Do not look for a workaround or a version from a random site. Tell Fin what you need and why. It can check whether the software is appropriate and do the difficult part.

## Use the Windows habit that still works: describe the job

You do not need to know the SP+ name for a feature before asking for it. Say what you are trying to accomplish. Fin can translate the Windows wording into the safe SP+ route.

Try one of these prompts:

- **"Fin, I used Windows for this. I need to [describe the task]. Show me the SP+ way."**
- **"Fin, this instruction is written for Windows. Is there a safe SP+ way to do it?"**
- **"Fin, this website wants me to download something. Do I need it, and can you handle the safe setup?"**

This is better than searching for a registry setting, a driver updater, or a repair download. Those are Windows answers to Windows problems. They are not automatically safe or useful on this computer.

## What not to carry over

Do not try to make SP+ behave like a copy of Windows. In particular:

- Do not download a cleaner, registry fixer, driver updater, or random installer to solve a problem.
- Do not follow a web page that tells you to type a technical command. Give the instruction to Fin and ask whether it applies.
- Do not turn off a protection just because a website or app asks. Ask Fin what the request means and what it changes.

This is not about taking control away from you. It is about putting the technical work with the tool that can inspect this specific computer before making a change.

## A simple first-week rule

Use the familiar apps and browser sites you need for work. When something feels different, pause before changing settings. Say the task out loud to Fin as if you were asking a colleague beside you. It can tell you where to go, carry out a repair, or explain why a Windows instruction does not fit.

title: Finding your way around
markdown:
# Finding your way around

You do not need to memorize the whole desktop. Learn the few places that answer most ordinary questions, then use Fin when a task does not match what you see. SP+ is set up so the useful controls are together rather than scattered through technical screens.

## The panel is your quick map

The desktop panel contains four everyday things:

- **The Applications menu** opens the list of programs, including Fin, Dolphin, your browser, and System Settings.
- **Your open apps** appear there while you work. Choose one to return to its window instead of opening another copy.
- **The small status controls** show everyday computer matters such as connections and sound.
- **The clock** is at the end of the panel.

You do not need to know the names of these parts. If someone tells you to use an unfamiliar item, ask Fin: **"Fin, where is [name of the thing] on my desktop?"**

## Open the right app for the job

Two apps matter more than their names suggest:

| When you want to | Open | Why |
|---|---|---|
| See, organize, or open a file | **Dolphin** | This is the SP+ file manager, like File Explorer in Windows |
| Change a computer setting | **System Settings** | This is where computer-wide choices live |

The browser is for the websites where much of your work happens. A browser setting belongs inside the browser. A setting that affects the computer as a whole belongs in System Settings. If that distinction is unclear, say what you want to change and let Fin point you to the right place.

## Do not turn a small problem into a maze

When something looks different from what you expected, pause before changing several settings. Make one visible change, check whether it solved the problem, then decide what to do next. If the screen, sound, printer, or connection is involved, Fin can inspect the computer instead of making you guess.

Useful prompts include:

- **"Fin, I cannot find the setting for [task]. Show me the right place."**
- **"Fin, this part of my desktop looks different. Tell me what it is before I change anything."**
- **"Fin, [sound, printer, display, or connection] is not working. Check it and explain the next safe step."**

## What belongs in a window and what belongs on the computer

An app's own choices affect that app. For example, a website's account choice or a document's font belongs inside the browser or document window. A computer-wide choice, such as how the screen looks or which device plays sound, belongs in System Settings or with the small status controls.

This distinction saves time. It also prevents a harmless browser task from becoming a hunt through every computer setting.

## When you are finished

Close the window you are done with, or leave it open if you expect to return to it. Return to the panel for the next app. If an app stops responding or you are unsure whether it is safe to close, ask Fin before forcing anything.

title: What this computer is
markdown:
# What this computer is

SP+ is the operating system on this work computer. It may look unfamiliar after Windows, but daily work is familiar: browser, documents, files, printing, and calls. You do not need Linux knowledge or commands to use it well.

## What SP+ is designed to protect

When this computer is turned off, the storage holding your work is encrypted. Someone who takes the laptop cannot simply remove the drive and read the files on it. Encryption does not protect a document you send to the wrong person, copy to an unprotected drive, or leave visible on an unlocked screen.

## Why a normal mistake is less likely to become a disaster

SP+ keeps its core operating system separate from your work. It uses a complete system image instead of letting ordinary programs rewrite the core a little at a time. That makes routine changes safer and gives a repair a clear starting point.

Hardware can fail, a website can be down, a file can be deleted, and a printer can still be stubborn. It does mean you should not have to gamble on random downloads or technical instructions to recover.

## Use Fin for the difficult part

**Fin is the assistant built into SP+.** Use it for non-sensitive questions or limited computer checks. It can inspect and change the computer. Ask it to explain before a change, but that does not guarantee every action waits for approval.

A Fin question can go to a connected AI provider. Do not paste a password, recovery key, client name, account number, client document, copied email, or full screenshot into a request.

Describe the outcome or problem in your own words. Start with one of these:

- **"Fin, I am new to SP+. Show me where I should go to [task]."**
- **"Fin, [plain description of the problem]. Check this computer, explain what you find, and do not change anything yet."**
- **"Fin, I need to [print, connect a device, or set up an app]. Explain the next step before changing anything."**

Read [Fin the assistant](asking-the-assistant.md) before relying on it for a difficult issue.

## What stays familiar

SP+ includes a web browser, LibreOffice for documents and spreadsheets, and printer tools. The names and layout may differ from Windows, but the tasks do not. [Finding your way around](getting-around.md) points out the parts you will use most often.

The browser's own password saver is deliberately turned off. Do not assume that a password manager is already installed or signed in. Read [Browser and passwords](brave-and-bitwarden.md) before saving credentials in a second place.

## Updates arrive in the background

SP+ checks and prepares a newer system version in the background. It does not restart the computer in the middle of an appointment. When a notice says a new version is ready, save your work and use a normal **Restart** or **Shut Down** at a suitable break. That completes the prepared update.

You do not need to find an operating-system installer or turn an update setting on. If something behaves differently after restarting, do not keep retrying or download a repair tool. Record what changed, then read [Something broke after an update: going back](../troubleshooting/going-back-after-an-update.md).

## Related pages

- [Coming from Windows](coming-from-windows.md)
- [Finding your way around](getting-around.md)
- [Updates and restarts](updates-and-restarts.md)

title: Your first day: what Welcome set up
markdown:
# Your first day: what Welcome set up

Welcome guides the first useful choices. Each part is separate, so do what helps today, skip the rest, and return later.

## Start with the things that make work easier

Welcome can help choose a desktop look, find the basic apps, read help inside the app, and open Fin. Preview a look, then confirm only if you want it. If a verified preview is unavailable, your current look remains.

## What Welcome can help with

| Need | What Welcome does |
|---|---|
| Find your way around | Shows the desktop map and the in-app help topics |
| Bring Fin into your work | Opens Fin in its own window so it can help with the hard parts |
| Check an office folder | Makes a temporary connection check, then removes that connection when the check ends |
| Test a printer | Checks the print service and sends one test page only when a printer is ready |
| Start email | Opens your provider's own web sign-in page |
| Add an optional tool | Offers Bitwarden and Signal as separate choices |

Welcome does not need to be the place where you solve every problem. Use it to start a task, then bring Fin in when the next step is unclear.

## Be clear about office connections

The office-folder step is a **check**, not a permanent drive left open on your computer. Have the office server name, shared-folder name, and office username ready. If you choose to save the folder credentials, Welcome uses the desktop wallet. If you do not know those details, do not guess or borrow someone else's login. Ask Fin: **"Fin, I need to check my office folder. What information should I have before I start?"**

The printer step sends exactly one test page after checking that the print service and a printer are ready. The email step opens the provider's own sign-in page. **Welcome does not ask for or store your email password.**

## Let Fin take the hard parts

Open Fin from Welcome when a task is technical, unclear, or simply not worth fighting alone. Describe the job, not the jargon. For example:

- **"Fin, I am setting up this work computer. What should I do first?"**
- **"Fin, I need to connect to the office folder. Tell me what you need from me, then handle the technical part."**
- **"Fin, I need Bitwarden for work logins. Help me set it up without creating duplicate password stores."**

If Fin asks you to connect a provider, follow its on-screen guidance. It does not need a key or password from an email. Do not give Fin client records, passwords, recovery information, or a sensitive document as a first test.

## What can wait

Bitwarden and Signal are optional tools. Adding them is your choice, not a requirement to finish Welcome. The same applies to the office-folder check, printer test, and email sign-in. A skipped step means "not today," not "broken."

When you do add something, keep the result simple: confirm that it opens or the one test page prints. If it does not, ask Fin what it found instead of repeating the setup several times.

## Return when you need it

You can reopen **SP+ Welcome** from **Applications** at any time. Return for help, to review a skipped office task, to open Fin, or to make another optional choice. Closing Welcome does not close Fin.

title: Backups: what is protected and what is not
markdown:
# Backups: what is protected and what is not

**This verified SP+ image does not include an automatic backup program.** Do not mistake disk encryption, a system update rollback, a File Portal copy, or a USB drive for a confirmed backup of your work.

## What each protection actually does

| Protection or copy | Helps with | Does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| Disk encryption | Someone taking the powered-off computer | Recovery after deletion, a bad save, or drive failure |
| Going back after an update | Returning the operating system to an earlier version | Restoring your Documents or other personal files |
| File Portal | Keeping a file in the online file service | That the service's backup, retention, or recovery policy covers your need |
| USB or external drive | Making a separate copy | That the copy is encrypted, current, or the only copy you need |

The computer's protected system image is not a time machine for your work. Your documents live separately from that system image. If you delete or overwrite a document, going back after an update does not bring it back.

## What is missing today

No installed backup or file-sync client, and no scheduled backup service, was found in the current verified SP+ image. That is a product gap, not a task for you to solve by downloading a random backup program.

Until your practice has an approved backup arrangement, keep important work in an approved location and make an independent copy deliberately. Do not claim a client file is protected just because it exists in Documents, the File Portal, or on a USB drive.

## The one test that matters

A backup is useful only if you can open the copy when the original is unavailable. After making an approved independent copy:

1. **Open the copy from the other location.** Check that it is the right file and complete.
2. **Keep the original until that check succeeds.** Do not replace one uncertainty with another.
3. **Know who owns the backup process.** You, your practice, or a named service provider should be able to answer where copies are kept and how a file is recovered.

This is a working habit, not a compliance certification. Retention, client-data handling, and recovery responsibilities belong to your practice's policy.

## Let Fin help with the hard part

Fin can inspect this computer and help you understand what is present. Start with a non-destructive question:

- **"Fin, check whether this computer has a backup configured. Do not install or change anything."**
- **"Fin, help me understand what copies of this work file I should verify. Do not move or delete anything."**
- **"Fin, I need an approved backup plan for client work. Tell me the decisions I need from my practice before changing this computer."**

Do not give Fin passwords, recovery information, client records, or document contents. Ask it to check the computer and explain the options first.

## If a file is already missing

Stop making changes in the folder where it was last seen. Do not assume a restart, update rollback, or re-downloading an app restores the document. Ask Fin for a diagnosis promptly, then use [Getting more help](../advisor-help/getting-more-help.md) if the file matters to client work.

## Related pages

- [Where your files live](where-your-files-live.md)
- [The file portal](the-file-portal.md)
- [USB drives and external storage](usb-and-external-drives.md)
- [Fin the assistant](../advisor-help/asking-the-assistant.md)

title: Private and Shared: the rule that stops misfiling
markdown:
# Private and Shared: the rule that stops misfiling

This rule is simple and important: **Private is for you alone. Shared - your name is for you and SecureProspective.** Choose the folder by who needs access, not by which name feels more convenient.

## Ask one question before you file anything

**Does SecureProspective need this file to do a specific piece of work?**

- **No. Put it in Private.** It is your file alone.
- **Yes. Put it in Shared - your name.** That is the place for a file you intend to make available to SecureProspective.

If the answer is unclear, do not guess. Keep the file where it is for the moment and ask Fin to explain the choice. It is better to take a minute before filing than to untangle access after the fact.

## What each folder means

| Folder | Who can access it | Typical reason to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Private** | You alone | A file SecureProspective does not need to see |
| **Shared - your name** | You and SecureProspective | A file you want SecureProspective to access for a named purpose |

Shared does not mean "put every client file here." It also does not mean an email attachment, a public link, or an instruction to send a file to someone outside SecureProspective. It is one deliberate access choice inside the File Portal.

## Use Fin before a difficult choice

Fin can turn a vague filing question into a clear next step. Tell it the work purpose, not the client details:

- **"Fin, SecureProspective needs to [purpose]. Should this file go in Private or Shared? Explain why before I move it."**
- **"Fin, I received a document that SecureProspective asked me to review. Help me decide where it belongs. Do not move it yet."**
- **"Fin, I am not sure who can see this folder. Explain the Private and Shared rule in plain language."**

Do not paste a client name, account number, password, recovery information, or document contents into the question. Fin needs the purpose of the file, not the private material inside it.

## If you think you chose the wrong folder

Stop before creating more copies or deleting anything. If a file may be in Shared when it should be Private, ask Fin or [Getting more help](../advisor-help/getting-more-help.md) promptly. Say which folder you chose and the file's purpose, not the client details. Do not assume moving a file back and forth fixes the access question.

## What this rule does not decide

Private and Shared decide the intended audience inside the File Portal. They do not answer whether a file is backed up, whether it is safe to send by email, or whether another copy exists on your computer. Those are separate decisions. Keep a clear local filing habit and use the portal deliberately.

## Related pages

- [The file portal](the-file-portal.md)
- [Where your files live](where-your-files-live.md)
- [Backups: what is protected and what is not](backups.md)
- [Fin the assistant](../advisor-help/asking-the-assistant.md)

title: The file portal
markdown:
# The file portal

The File Portal is the online place for client files: **cloud.secureprospective.com**. It opens in your browser and has its own sign-in page. It is not the same thing as the Documents folder on this computer, and it does not automatically turn every local file into an online one.

## What the File Portal is for

Use the portal when a client file needs to be kept in the SecureProspective file service instead of passed around in email attachments. It is a web service, so it needs an internet connection and your portal access. Welcome checks whether the service is ready before opening its details.

Your portal password is separate from your computer sign-in and from a back-office password. Do not reuse a password just because the names feel related. If you cannot sign in, do not keep guessing. Ask Fin to help you identify whether the problem is the portal, the browser, or this computer.

## Private and Shared are different places

The portal shows two important destinations:

- **Private** is for you alone.
- **Shared - your name** is for you and SecureProspective.

That difference is not cosmetic. It decides who can access a file. Read [Private and Shared: the rule that stops misfiling](private-and-shared.md) before you upload or move client work. If you are in doubt, leave the file where it is and ask Fin to explain the choice before you act.

## Opening the portal safely

Open **SP+ Welcome**, choose the **File Portal** service, and let it hand you to the browser. You can also go directly to **cloud.secureprospective.com** when you know you are using the correct address. The portal redirects to its sign-in page when you are not already signed in.

Before you put a file there, check these three things:

1. **The file is the final copy you intend to share or keep online.** Open it once before uploading.
2. **You chose Private or Shared on purpose.** Never use Shared just because it is more visible.
3. **You know whether a local copy still exists.** A downloaded or uploaded copy may need its own filing decision in Documents.

## Let Fin remove the uncertainty

Fin can help with the computer side of the task without needing your portal password or a client document. Try one of these prompts:

- **"Fin, I need to access the File Portal. What do I need before I sign in?"**
- **"Fin, I need to put a client file in the portal. Explain Private and Shared before I move anything."**
- **"Fin, the File Portal will not open. Check my computer and browser connection, then explain what you find."**

Do not paste a password, recovery information, client name, account number, or document contents into a request. If Fin asks for information that looks sensitive, stop and describe the problem without it.

## When the portal is not ready

A service can be temporarily unavailable even when the rest of your computer works. If Welcome says the File Portal is not ready, retry once after checking your normal internet connection. If it still fails, ask Fin for a diagnosis or use [Getting more help](../advisor-help/getting-more-help.md). Do not work around the problem by sending a client file to a personal email account.

title: USB drives and external storage
markdown:
# USB drives and external storage

A USB stick, external hard drive, or portable SSD is separate storage. Treat it as a place to copy files deliberately, not as an extension of your computer that is always private, encrypted, or backed up.

## What should happen when you plug one in

SP+ includes the services Dolphin needs for removable storage and common drive formats. Normally, a recognized drive appears in **Dolphin** or through a device notice. Open it there to see its name and contents.

If a drive does not appear, do not install a driver or download a repair tool. First check that the cable is firmly connected and, for an external hard drive, that it has power. Then ask Fin: **"Fin, I plugged in an external drive and cannot see it. Check what this computer detects."**

## Copy files deliberately

Before copying client work to a drive, ask three questions:

1. **Why does this copy need to leave the computer?** A temporary transfer, a handoff, and a backup are different jobs.
2. **Who will have the drive?** A USB stick can be misplaced or plugged into another computer.
3. **Where is the original?** Keep a known local copy until you have confirmed the copy on the drive opens correctly.

Use Dolphin to copy the file, wait for the copy to finish, then open the copied file from the drive once. A file that has a familiar name is not proof that it copied completely.

## Remove the drive safely

When you are done, use the safe-removal control Dolphin shows for the drive. Wait until it says the drive can be removed, then unplug it. Do not pull a drive out while a copy is in progress or while an app is still saving to it. That can leave a file incomplete or damage the drive's file list.

If you cannot tell whether a copy finished or where the removal control is, ask Fin before unplugging: **"Fin, help me safely remove this USB drive. Do not change or delete any files."**

## Do not assume the drive has this computer's protections

The storage inside this computer is encrypted when it is powered off. A USB drive is its own device. Do not assume it has the same protection, password, backup, or access rules.

Do not keep the only copy of important work on a USB drive. Do not leave one in a laptop bag, car, printer, or conference room. If you need an encrypted external drive or a practice-approved way to transfer client material, ask Fin or support before using the drive for client files.

## When a drive asks you to do something unexpected

Stop if the computer asks to format, erase, initialize, or repair a drive you expected to contain files. Those choices can be destructive. Ask Fin what it sees and what each choice would do before approving anything.

Useful prompt: **"Fin, this external drive is asking to be formatted or repaired. I expected files on it. Explain what you see before changing anything."**

title: Where your files live
markdown:
# Where your files live

Your everyday files live in your personal home area. You do not need to know its technical name or location. Open **Dolphin**, the Files app, and use the folders you can see there. When this computer is off, that area is on encrypted storage.

## The three folders to recognize

| Folder | Use it for | Do not assume |
|---|---|---|
| **Documents** | Work you want to keep and find again | Saving here does not automatically share or back up a file |
| **Downloads** | Files you just received from a website or email | A download is not organized, reviewed, or ready to send onward |
| **Documents/Fin** | Files Fin creates for you | It is still your job to check the result before using or sharing it |

**Documents** is the sensible local starting point for a letter, spreadsheet, PDF, or working copy. **Downloads** is a landing area. Move a file out of Downloads once you know where it belongs, then check that the copy you need opens before deleting anything.

## What Fin does with files it creates

Fin saves documents it creates in **Documents/Fin**. That keeps its work visible in the same place as your other documents instead of hidden inside an app. Open Dolphin and look in Documents when Fin tells you it made a file.

Fin can help you create or find a file, but it should not make a filing decision about client material without you. Use a clear request such as:

- **"Fin, create a draft for me and save it in Documents/Fin."**
- **"Fin, help me find the file about [description]. Do not move, rename, or delete anything."**
- **"Fin, I need to file this client document. Explain whether it belongs in Private or Shared before we move it."**

Do not paste client information, passwords, recovery information, or a document's contents into a request just to identify a file. Describe it by its purpose instead.

## Local, shared, and online are different choices

Putting a file in Documents keeps a local copy on this computer. It does not decide who else can see it. A shared office folder and the File Portal are separate places with their own access rules. Before moving client work, decide who needs access, then read [Private and Shared: the rule that stops misfiling](private-and-shared.md).

A local copy may be useful even after you share a file elsewhere. It is also another copy to manage. Do not assume that encryption means every copy is backed up, that a shared copy is private, or that deleting one copy deletes the others.

## A simple filing habit

When you save or receive a file:

1. **Name it so you can recognize it later.** Use a clear purpose and date where that helps.
2. **Put the working copy in Documents.** Do not leave important work buried in Downloads.
3. **Decide whether it is Private or Shared before you move it again.** This is a client-data decision, not an app setting.
4. **Open the saved copy once.** Make sure it is the file you expected before closing the original.

If you are unsure, stop before making extra copies or deleting the original. Fin can help you inspect the situation and choose the next safe step.

title: Browser and passwords
markdown:
# Browser and passwords

**Brave** is the web browser on SP+. Use it for the business websites you already rely on. Its built-in password saver and credit-card autofill are deliberately turned off, so a password does not end up copied into several places by accident.

## What the browser is set up not to do

Brave's work-computer setup turns off its Rewards, Wallet, VPN, browser AI chat, and several promotional or reporting features. Those are not services you need to turn back on to do normal work. If a website points you toward a browser wallet, an AI chat, or an unfamiliar extension, pause and ask Fin before adding anything.

The browser still opens ordinary websites, webmail, carrier portals, CRMs, e-signature tools, and video calls. A protection being on is not a sign that the site is broken.

## Passwords need one deliberate home

The verified SP+ image does **not** include Bitwarden by default. SP+ Welcome offers Bitwarden as an optional addition when your practice wants it. Do not assume it is already installed, signed in, or holding your passwords.

Choose one approved password manager and use it consistently. Do not let a browser, a note, and a second password tool all remember the same login. If a site offers to save a password in the browser, decline it and use the password method your practice approved instead.

Never give a password, recovery code, or client account information to Fin. Fin can help with the computer and explain the safe route, but you enter your own sign-in details only into the service you intend to use.

## Use Bitwarden only when you are ready

If your practice uses Bitwarden, add it through **SP+ Welcome** and sign in with your own account when you are ready. Start with one non-sensitive work login so you can confirm that the account and password method are correct before relying on it for every site.

Ask Fin for guidance without sharing the secret itself:

- **"Fin, my practice uses Bitwarden. Help me add it through SP+ Welcome and tell me what I should check first."**
- **"Fin, this website wants to save my password in the browser. Explain the approved alternative without asking for my password."**
- **"Fin, I need a separate browser sign-in for [purpose]. Help me choose the safe route."**

## Before you sign in to a work site

Check the address in the browser before entering a password. Use a bookmark you trust or type the known address yourself. If a page appears suddenly, asks for a password again, or offers a download you did not expect, stop and ask Fin what it is before continuing.

Do not solve a browser problem by installing a random extension, cleaner, or Windows `.exe` file. SP+ has a safer software route, and Fin can help you use it.

## When a site needs something extra

A website may need a browser permission, a video-call setting, or approved software. Describe the outcome to Fin rather than guessing at a download: **"Fin, this work site needs [thing]. Check what is safe on this computer before I install or allow it."**

title: Email
markdown:
# Email

Use your practice's own webmail page for day-to-day email. SP+ Welcome can open the Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 sign-in page, but your password goes only into the provider's page. SP+ does not ask for or store your email password.

## Open your work email the safe way

In **SP+ Welcome**, open **Connect this computer to your office** and choose email. Select **Google Workspace** or **Microsoft 365**, then continue to the provider's sign-in page. Check the provider before entering your details.

After it opens the page, Welcome creates a local launcher for that provider in Applications, so you can return to the same webmail page later. The launcher opens the website. It does not connect, read, or manage your mailbox for you.

If your practice uses another email provider, Welcome does not guess which site to open. Ask your practice for the correct webmail address rather than trying a personal account or a search result.

## Why Thunderbird may open instead

**Thunderbird** is installed on SP+, but the verified starting setup has no email account connected to it. It is an option for a practice that deliberately chooses to set up a desktop email app, not a sign that your work mailbox should already be there.

Email-address links can open Thunderbird by default. If that happens while you use webmail, it does not mean anything is broken. Copy the address into a new webmail message, or ask Fin whether Thunderbird is approved before adding an account.

## Check before you attach or send

Email leaves the computer when you send it. Before attaching a file, check the recipient, the file name, and the version. Pause before replying to an unexpected request for client material, a password, or a document. Use a known contact method to confirm it if anything feels out of place.

Do not use a personal email account, a random file-sharing site, or a browser extension as a shortcut for client information. Save attachments in the right place first, then send only through the practice-approved service.

## Let Fin help, but keep sending in your hands

Fin can help you understand an email setup problem or prepare a draft, but you review and send every message yourself. Do not give Fin your email password or paste client names, account numbers, balances, documents, or message contents into a request.

Useful prompts include:

- **"Fin, my Google Workspace sign-in page will not open. Check the computer-side problem before I change anything."**
- **"Fin, help me make a short email template about [non-sensitive topic]. Do not send it."**
- **"Fin, Thunderbird opened when I clicked an email address. Explain the approved next step without setting up an account yet."**

## If you cannot sign in

Start again from the known provider page. If the password is rejected, use the provider's recovery process or contact the person who manages practice email. Do not send a password to Fin or type it into a page you reached through an unexpected pop-up or link.

If the provider page itself will not load, ask Fin before installing anything or changing browser settings. A sign-in problem is not a reason to download a random mail program.

title: Installing software safely
markdown:
# Installing software safely

Use SP+ Welcome, **Discover**, or Fin when you need software. Do not treat a search result, browser pop-up, or Windows `.exe` file as the normal way to add an app. The safe route is visible and gives you a result you can check.

## Decide what job the app must do

Start with the outcome, not an app name. For example: "I need to join a client call," "I need a password manager," or "I need to scan from the office copier." Check with your practice before using any app for client work. An open software library is not a practice-approved list.

If the app will see client information, sign into an account, send a message, or connect to a service, ask what your practice approves before installing it. The right app for personal use is not automatically right for work.

## Use the named optional tools when they fit

In **SP+ Welcome**, open **Optional tools + store**. It offers **Bitwarden** and **Signal Desktop** as named optional additions. They install only when you choose their own add button. Welcome checks that the app is actually present before it says the installation is ready.

Bitwarden is for work logins when your practice uses it. Signal is an optional communication tool, not a substitute for your practice's decision about client communication. Do not add either one because a website or another person told you to without checking the work need first.

## Browse Discover, not the open web

The same Welcome screen can open **Discover**, the software library. It checks that the configured Flathub source is available before opening Discover. If that source is not available, Welcome reports that instead of pretending the store opened.

Discover lets you browse available apps, but browsing is not approval. Read what an app does, check the publisher, and ask your practice before using it for client work. If you find an app you want, write down its name and the job it would do before asking for help.

## Zoom is supplied as an SP+ base app

Zoom is supplied through SP+'s base-app setup, rather than something you need to find on a website. Check Applications first. If it has not appeared yet, ask Fin to check the safe next step instead of downloading another copy.

For a different call, scanner, signing, or business app, do not assume that an installer from a search result is the right version or the right approval path.

## Keep random installers out

Do not download a Windows `.exe`, a Mac `.dmg`, a browser extension, a driver disc, or a command copied from a web page to solve a work problem. Do not enter a password into an installer or pop-up you did not expect.

If a website claims you must install something immediately, pause. Open Fin and describe the outcome and the site name, without sharing a password or client information.

## Ask Fin for a checked route

Fin can check what is already installed and help with the safe installation path. Tell it what you need to accomplish and ask it to explain the change before it makes one. For example:

- **"Fin, I need a way to [task]. Check whether this computer already has it, then explain the approved next step before installing anything."**
- **"Fin, this site says I need [app]. Tell me whether it is safe and necessary for this computer before I add it."**

title: Keyboard shortcuts
markdown:
# Keyboard shortcuts

You do not need to memorize shortcuts to use SP+. The useful ones are the same familiar combinations from Windows and most work apps. Learn one or two that save you time; there is no prize for using the keyboard instead of the mouse.

## Copy, paste, and undo

These work in Writer, Calc, Brave, and most other apps:

| Keys | What they do |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+C** | Copy the selected text, file, or item |
| **Ctrl+X** | Cut the selected item so you can move it |
| **Ctrl+V** | Paste what you copied or cut |
| **Ctrl+Z** | Undo the last change |
| **Ctrl+A** | Select everything in the current document, box, or page |

Copying is usually safer than cutting when you are unsure. Paste into the new place, check that it arrived, then remove the original only if you meant to move it.

## Save, find, and print

| Keys | What they do |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+S** | Save your current work |
| **Ctrl+F** | Find a word or phrase in the current page or document |
| **Ctrl+P** | Open the print window |

Use **Ctrl+S** before closing a document, especially before attaching it to an email or uploading it. **Ctrl+F** is often faster than scrolling through a long PDF, web page, or spreadsheet. **Ctrl+P** opens the print choices; check the printer name and page range before you send anything.

## Move between open work

**Alt+Tab** switches between open windows. Hold **Alt** and tap **Tab** until the window you want is selected, then let go. This is useful when you are moving between a browser, a document, and an email without losing your place.

The key with the Windows logo is called the **Meta** key here. Press it by itself to open the Applications menu and start typing the name of an app. **Meta+D** shows the desktop, and **Meta+L** locks the screen immediately when you step away.

## Take a screenshot carefully

Press **Print Screen** to open SP+'s screenshot capture tool. Choose only the part of the screen you need. A screenshot can contain client names, account numbers, email previews, or browser tabs just as easily as a document can.

Before sharing one, look at it closely. Do not share private information in it or paste it into Fin, a public website, or an unapproved support chat. If you only need to show a technical error, capture the error itself rather than the whole desktop.

## If a shortcut surprises you

A shortcut may behave differently inside a particular website or app. That is normal. Use the menu instead, or ask Fin: **"Fin, I pressed [keys] in [app] and got [result]. Explain what happened without changing anything."**

You never need a shortcut to open a command line on SP+. If a help page or website tells you to type a command, stop and ask Fin for the safe route instead.

title: LibreOffice: your Word and Excel
markdown:
# LibreOffice: your Word and Excel

SP+ includes LibreOffice for everyday documents and spreadsheets. **Writer** is the Word equivalent. **Calc** is the Excel equivalent. They are already installed, and the verified SP+ setup is configured to use Word and Excel formats for new work unless you deliberately choose another format.

## Start with the right app

Open **LibreOffice Writer** for letters, proposals, notes, and other documents. Open **LibreOffice Calc** for lists, calculations, budgets, and spreadsheets. You can find both in the Applications menu, or open a file from Dolphin and choose the appropriate app.

The names and controls are different from Microsoft Office, but the work is familiar: write, save, print, and share. Do not spend ten minutes looking for an exact Windows button. Tell Fin what you are trying to do and ask where that action lives in Writer or Calc.

## Save in a format others can open

Writer is configured to save new documents as Word `.docx` files, and Calc is configured to save new spreadsheets as Excel `.xlsx` files. The installed LibreOffice can also create those formats directly.

Before you send an important file:

1. **Save it with a clear name in Documents.** Keep the original working copy.
2. **Check the ending of the file name.** Use `.docx` for a Word document or `.xlsx` for an Excel spreadsheet when that is what the recipient expects.
3. **Open the saved copy once.** Check the first and last page, or the important spreadsheet tabs, before sharing it.

A familiar file ending is useful, but it is not a substitute for looking at the result.

## Treat complex files carefully

This manual has not verified every complicated Microsoft Office file. A document with unusual fonts, embedded objects, macros, complex formulas, or elaborate page layout deserves a careful review before it goes to a client or colleague.

Keep the original file. Work on a copy when possible. If something looks different after saving, stop before repeatedly saving over it. Ask Fin to explain the difference or ask support before changing the document again.

## Let Fin help without risking the original

Fin is useful for the difficult parts: finding a feature, drafting a new document, or helping you review what to check. It saves documents it creates in **Documents/Fin**, so your original work stays separate.

Try one of these prompts:

- **"Fin, I need to [describe the task] in Writer or Calc. Show me the safe SP+ way."**
- **"Fin, make a new draft in Documents/Fin for [purpose]. Do not change my existing file."**
- **"Fin, this Word or Excel file looks different after I saved it. Help me decide what to check before I share it."**

Do not paste client data, passwords, or the whole document into a request just to ask about formatting.

## When a document needs to be a PDF

Use the PDF page when you need a read-only copy, a form, or a signature workflow. A Word or Excel file is for editing; a PDF is usually for preserving the finished appearance.

title: PDFs: reading, filling in, signing
markdown:
# PDFs: reading, filling in, signing

PDFs open in **Okular**, the document viewer included with SP+. Double-click a PDF in Files to open it. Treat the original as something to read and preserve, not casually rewrite.

## Read and check a PDF

Use Okular to read a PDF, move between pages, and search for a word or name. Before sending one, check the page count and the pages with signatures, amounts, dates, or client instructions. A normal-looking preview can still omit a final page or attachment.

If you need to mark up a copy for your own review, keep the original unchanged. Use **File**, then **Save As** to make a clearly named working copy first. Reopen the saved copy before sharing it so you know the changes are actually there.

## Fill in a PDF form when it has fields

Some PDFs contain real fillable fields. When Okular detects them, it shows a form notice above the document. Choose **Show Forms**, or use **View** then **Show Forms**, to enter information in those fields.

Not every blank line in a PDF is a form field. If you do not see the form option or cannot click into the expected box, stop rather than forcing text into the page. Ask the sender for a fillable version, or use the approved signing service for that document. Do not upload a client PDF to a free online converter just to make it editable.

After entering information, use **File**, then **Save As** for a new copy. Open that copy again and check that the entries remained before you send it. If it offers an Okular archive instead of a PDF, stop and ask Fin before sending it.

## Know which kind of signature you need

"Sign a PDF" can mean two different things:

- An **e-signature request** usually comes from a service your practice already uses. Open the request from the known sender or official service page, review the document, and complete the signing process there.
- A **digital certificate signature** is a technical certificate attached to the PDF. Okular can inspect an existing PDF signature and includes a **Tools** option to digitally sign a PDF, but it needs a signing certificate already provided to the computer. Okular does not create that certificate for you.

If you are unsure which is required, ask the sender or Fin before changing the file. Follow the signing method the sender requires.

## Keep client documents in the right place

Save a working PDF where the right people can see it. **Private** is for you alone. **Shared** is for files SecureProspective needs to see. Before attaching or uploading it, confirm the file name, recipient, and final version. A second copy is easier to make than to retrieve a wrong one after it leaves your control.

Do not give Fin a client PDF, its contents, a password, or a signing certificate. You can still ask for general guidance: **"Fin, this PDF is supposed to have form fields. Explain how I can check that in Okular without opening or uploading the document."**

## When Okular is not enough

A protected form, e-signature platform, or certificate requirement may need approved software or a service. Do not guess at an installer or website. Ask Fin: **"Fin, I need an approved way to [read, fill, or sign] a PDF. Explain the safe next step before adding or changing anything."**

title: Printing
markdown:
# Printing

Printing from a normal app works much as it did on Windows. SP+ has its print service ready, but your office printer still needs to be identified and set up for this particular computer before it can receive a document.

## Print an everyday document

In Writer, Calc, a PDF reader, or most other apps, choose **File**, then **Print**, or use **Ctrl+P**. Check the printer name, the page range, and the number of copies before sending it. When a document contains client information, pause for that check. Sending a page to the wrong printer is an easy mistake to make and hard to undo.

If the printer you expect is already in the list, select it and print normally. If no printer is listed, do not keep retrying the same document. It needs to be set up first.

## Find the printer settings

Open the Applications menu and search for **Print Settings**. This is where the computer lists printers it already knows and where an office printer can be added.

Only add a printer you can identify. A shared office network can show several similar names. Use the name on the physical printer or its location, such as "reception" or "upstairs office", rather than guessing from a technical-looking address. If you cannot tell which one is yours, ask Fin before choosing one.

Do not download a driver, a browser extension, or a Windows `.exe` file to make a printer work. That is a common detour, not the safe route on this computer.

## Send one test page before important work

SP+ Welcome has a printer check in **Connect this computer to your office**. Choose **Print one test page** after the intended printer has been set up. Welcome checks for a usable printer first, then sends exactly one test-page job.

The result tells you whether the print system accepted the job. Pick up or look at the page before sending a proposal or a client record. A plain test page is a better test than a confidential document.

## If the printer is already set up but nothing arrives

Check the physical printer first: it needs power, paper, and no error message or jam showing on its own screen. Then check that the correct printer was selected in the print window.

If those checks fail, ask Fin and name the printer by location. Before any repair, ask which printer it sees. Its current scripted repair uses **Advisor Test Printer**, a test fixture, not office hardware. If that is all it names, it has not proved the office printer works.

Try a prompt such as:

- **"Fin, the printer by reception is not printing. Check the queue and printer state first, then tell me what you found."**
- **"Fin, I need to add the printer in the upstairs office. Check what this computer can see, tell me which one you plan to add, and ask before changing anything."**

Do not include a client name, document contents, password, or account information in the request. The printer location and the problem are enough to start.

## If you need a different kind of help

A printer may need a network connection, a setting in the app, or an approved change on the computer. Describe the outcome to Fin instead of trying random downloads: **"Fin, this document needs to print on [printer location]. Check the safe next step."**

title: Scanning documents
markdown:
# Scanning documents

SP+ includes the underlying support needed to find compatible scanners, but the verified starting image does not include a scanning app or a Scan icon. That is deliberate and honest: scanner models and office workflows differ, so the right setup needs to match the device you actually use.

## Start with the outcome, not a download

Before setting anything up, decide what the finished file needs to be. For most paper records, that means a readable PDF saved in the right place. Decide whether it belongs in **Private** or **Shared** before you scan it. Do not use a client document as a test page.

If the device is a printer with a scanner on top, the scanning side is a separate job from printing. A printer that can make copies or receive a print job is not proof that this computer is ready to receive scans from it.

## Ask Fin to check the device first

Tell Fin the make and model if you know it, whether it is connected by USB or on the office network, and where it is located. Fin can check whether the computer can see the device and recommend the safe next step. Ask for an explanation before any app or setting is added.

Use a prompt such as:

- **"Fin, I need to scan from the copier by reception. Check whether this computer can see it and explain the safe next step before changing anything."**
- **"Fin, this USB scanner is a [make and model]. Check compatibility and ask me before installing or changing anything."**

You do not need to send Fin the document, a client name, a password, or account information to get help with scanner setup.

## Do not assume the printer screen is the safe route

Many multifunction devices offer choices such as scan to email, cloud storage, USB, or a network folder. Those choices can send a copy somewhere outside the computer. Do not choose an unfamiliar destination for a client document just because it is convenient. Ask Fin or your practice first which destination is approved.

If a device asks for an office email password, cloud password, or folder password, stop before entering it. Use the practice's approved setup route, not a password copied into an unfamiliar printer screen.

## Once scanning is set up

Use a plain, non-sensitive page for the first test. Then open the saved result and check that every page is present, readable, and facing the right way before you file or send it.

Put the finished file in the place you chose before scanning. **Private** is for you alone. **Shared** is for files SecureProspective needs to see. If the scan is going to a client or another service, confirm the recipient and file before sending it.

## If the computer cannot see the scanner

Do not download a driver from a search result or try random browser add-ons. Scanner compatibility is specific to the model and connection. Tell Fin the model, whether the scanner is plugged in or on the same office network, and what you were trying to do. Fin can narrow down whether the next step is connection, approved software, or a practice setup decision.

title: Scheduling social posts
markdown:
# Scheduling social posts

Social scheduling happens on the **SecureProspective Social** site, not inside the computer itself. SP+ Welcome checks whether that service is available and opens it in your browser. It does not connect an account, write a post, or schedule anything on your behalf.

## Start from Welcome and check availability

Open **SP+ Welcome** and go to **Your services**. The Social card checks the service before it lets you open it. When the card says it is ready, open it and complete sign-in, account connections, and scheduling on the Social site.

A ready card means the service answered the availability check. It does not mean your own social account is connected or that a post has been published. Check those things on the Social site itself.

If Social is still being set up, wait and try again later. If it is unavailable, use **Retry** after checking your internet connection. Welcome does not change any account while it is checking, so an unavailable result does not mean a connection was damaged.

## Connect only what is available

The Social card shows the platforms the service currently reports. A platform marked live is ready to connect on the Social site. A platform waiting for approval is not ready yet. Do not work around that status by adding a browser extension, sharing a password, or connecting through an unrelated service.

When you connect an account, read the service page carefully and use the account your practice approved. Keep the login and approval steps on the Social site. Welcome is only the safe starting point.

## Review a post before scheduling it

Treat a scheduled post like an email that will leave later. Before you schedule it, check the wording, audience, account, date, time, links, and any attached image. Make sure the draft has the practice approval it needs before you put it on a calendar.

Do not include client information, account details, or private meeting information in a post or an image. If a post mentions a client story, pause and use the practice's approval process before scheduling it.

## A schedule is not a guarantee

Social posts are scheduled, not guaranteed. If the service has an outage, it may not catch up a missed post automatically. Review the schedule after the service returns and decide whether to reschedule, revise, or leave the post alone.

The Social service is also not a compliance archive for SEC Marketing Rule purposes. Keep any required approvals, records, or evidence in the practice-approved place rather than assuming the scheduler is the record.

## Use Fin for preparation, not publication

Fin can help you turn a non-sensitive idea into a short draft or a checklist for reviewing a post. Keep the decision to approve and publish with you or the person your practice authorizes. Do not give Fin client names, account information, passwords, or connected-account details.

Try a prompt such as: **"Fin, turn this non-sensitive topic into a short social-post draft for my review. Do not post it or connect any account."**

title: Video calls, camera and microphone
markdown:
# Video calls, camera and microphone

SP+ includes the browser and audio-video services needed for browser-based calls. **Zoom** is an SP+ base app that is set up when the computer can reach its app source, so check Applications to see whether it is ready. Other meeting services normally run in **Brave**. A successful call still depends on the camera, microphone, headset, and service account available to you.

## Before the call starts

Connect a headset or external camera before opening the meeting page when you can. Then use the meeting service's own preview or test area to check what it sees. Look at the camera picture and say a few words into the microphone before joining, not while a client is waiting.

If your laptop has a physical camera cover, microphone mute switch, or headset mute button, check that first. Those controls override anything a website can do.

## Let the meeting site ask before you allow

A call website may ask to use the camera or microphone. Read the site name in the request and allow it only when it is the meeting service you intended to open. Do not grant camera or microphone access to an unexpected page, browser extension, or pop-up.

If the call page lets you choose devices, select the camera and microphone you are actually using. An unplugged headset or an old external camera can remain selected even after it is gone. If the picture or sound is wrong, leave the meeting page open and ask Fin to check the computer side before changing random settings.

## Keep the call private

Close unrelated client files and messages before joining. If the meeting service offers a choice, share the specific window you mean to show rather than the whole desktop. Check the preview and participant list before discussing client information.

Do not use an unapproved screen-recording, transcription, or browser add-on as a shortcut. Those tools can copy a meeting outside the call. Ask your practice before enabling one, even if another attendee says it is normal.

## When nobody can hear or see you

Start with the physical checks: camera cover open, microphone not muted, headset connected, and the correct device selected on the call page. If you can, leave and rejoin the meeting once after checking them.

Then ask Fin in plain words: **"Fin, nobody can see or hear me on this video call. Check the camera and microphone on this computer first, then tell me what you found."** Fin is set up to check whether the devices exist, are muted or disabled, are selected correctly, and whether the meeting app has permission. It can also offer a short test recording before the next call.

Do not give Fin meeting links, client names, account information, or a recording to diagnose the computer-side problem.

## If the call needs an app or screen sharing

Some practices use a dedicated call app or need a particular screen-sharing setup. Check Applications for Zoom before looking elsewhere. For another service, do not download an app from a search result or accept an unexpected browser prompt. Ask Fin: **"Fin, my practice needs [service] for video calls. Explain the approved next step before installing or allowing anything."**

title: Bluetooth devices
markdown:
# Bluetooth devices

Use Bluetooth for your own headset, speaker, keyboard, mouse, or similar accessory. Pair only a device you recognize. Do not use Bluetooth to send client documents, recordings, passwords, or other work information.

## Get the accessory ready

Charge the accessory or fit a fresh battery, then turn it on. Put it into pairing or discoverable mode using its instructions. Buttons and lights vary by model.

If it has recently been used with a phone or another computer, turn the accessory off and on before you begin. Some accessories try to reconnect to a previous device instead of appearing ready to pair.

## Open Bluetooth settings

Open **System Settings** from Applications and search for **Bluetooth**. SP+ includes the Bluetooth settings module and Bluetooth controls. Turn Bluetooth on there if it is off, then use the option to add a device when it appears.

Wait for the scan to show the accessory. Choose the name you recognize, not a nearby unknown device with a similar name. If both the computer and accessory show a pairing number, confirm it only when the numbers match. Cancel an unexpected pairing request or a number that does not match.

## If the device does not appear

Keep the accessory close to the computer while pairing. Confirm it is still in pairing mode, then retry the scan once. Do not change several settings or repeatedly remove devices while it is still searching.

If it is a keyboard or mouse you need to operate the computer, keep a wired or built-in input method available until pairing is complete. Do not lock yourself out of the controls by relying on an untested wireless device.

## If a known device will not reconnect

First turn the accessory off and back on. If you also use it with a phone or another computer, disconnect it there only if you own that device and it is safe to do so. Return to Bluetooth settings and try connecting the known device again.

If that does not help, use the settings page to forget the device, then pair it again from the start. Forgetting removes this computer's saved pairing for that accessory. It does not repair a flat battery, failed headset, or a device that is too far away.

## Headsets connected but no sound

A headset can be connected while sound is still set to the computer's speakers, or a call service can have a separate device choice. Open the volume control near the clock and select the headset if it is listed. Then check the call or media app's own audio settings.

Use a non-sensitive test sound or meeting preview. Do not play a client voicemail, recording, or private message just to test headphones. See [No sound](no-sound.md) for the full audio checks.

## When Bluetooth is unavailable

If Bluetooth settings show no adapter or no usable control, do not download a driver, extension, or Windows `.exe` file. Ask Fin: **"Fin, Bluetooth does not show an adapter on this computer. Check what hardware and service it can see before changing anything."** Include the accessory type and whether it ever worked on this computer, but not client information.

No Bluetooth adapter, pairing session, headset, speaker, keyboard, mouse, or file transfer was tested for this manual. A physical accessory or hardware-specific failure may need a direct check rather than more pairing attempts.

title: No sound
markdown:
# No sound

Start with the small checks before changing settings. Sound can be coming from the wrong place, muted in the app you are using, or blocked by a headset, monitor, or meeting service. You do not need to download a driver to try these steps.

## Check the physical sound path

Make sure speakers are powered if they have their own power switch. Check a headset cable is seated, the headset is charged if wireless, and any physical mute button is off. If you expected laptop speakers, unplug headphones or a dock once and see whether the sound returns.

Use the volume keys or the volume icon near the clock to make sure the computer is not muted and the volume is high enough to hear. Do this while a harmless sound is playing, such as a meeting service's test sound, so you can tell immediately whether the change helped.

## Choose where sound should come from

Click the volume icon near the clock and look for the current sound device. Choose the speakers, headphones, monitor, or dock you actually intend to use. A monitor connected by HDMI, a docking station, or a headset can become the selected sound device even when you are no longer using it.

After choosing a device, play one short, non-sensitive sound again. If it works, leave the selection alone. If it does not, do not cycle through every unfamiliar device name. Note the name of the one you expected and ask Fin.

## Check the app that is silent

A browser tab, video-call service, or media app can have its own mute and device settings. If sound works elsewhere but not in one app, open that app's audio or meeting settings and choose the same speaker or headset you selected for the computer.

For a call, check both sides: the computer's output selection and the meeting service's speaker setting. If only other people cannot hear you, also check the microphone selection and any physical microphone mute button.

## When no device is listed or sound stays silent

Do not install a driver, browser extension, or Windows `.exe` file because a sound prompt suggested it. SP+ already includes its audio service and volume controls. If no expected speaker, headset, or microphone appears, reconnect that device once and ask Fin what the computer can see.

Use a prompt such as: **"Fin, I have no sound from [speakers/headset/monitor]. Check the audio devices and current selection first, then tell me what you found."** For a call: **"Fin, nobody can hear me on a video call. Check the microphone and permissions before changing anything."**

Fin is set up to check whether a microphone or camera exists, is muted or disabled, is selected correctly, and is permitted for the meeting app. It can offer a short test recording before the next call.

## Keep the test private

Use a test sound, a meeting preview, or a non-sensitive video to check audio. Do not play a client voicemail, meeting recording, or private message just to prove that speakers work. Do not give Fin a recording, client name, or account information to diagnose a device problem.

title: Printer not printing
markdown:
# Printer not printing

Do not keep sending the same document when nothing comes out. Repeated copies can create a long queue or send a confidential file later, when you are no longer standing at the printer. Work through the checks below, then test with one plain page.

## Start at the physical printer

Check that the printer is on, awake, has paper, and is not showing a jam, open cover, toner, or other error on its own display. If it is a shared office printer, make sure you are at the one whose location matches the name you chose in the print window.

If the printer is clearly asleep, wake it and wait for its own display to say it is ready. Do not restart a printer at a client office or shared location unless you know it is yours to restart. Another person may have a job waiting.

## Check the document before you send it again

Open the print window in the app and look at the printer name, page range, and number of copies. Select the intended printer, not a similarly named device, fax entry, or old printer. Do not use a proposal or client record as a test.

If a print job is visibly waiting, give it a short moment to move. If it remains clearly stuck and you recognize it as your own job, use **Print Settings** to remove that job before sending a single test page. Do not cancel a job that belongs to someone else.

## Use one test page

After the printer is set up, SP+ Welcome can send **one test page** from **Connect this computer to your office**. It checks for a usable printer first and reports whether the print system accepted the job.

Look at the physical printer and collect the page before you treat the result as a success. A computer can accept a job while the paper is still blocked, the wrong printer was selected, or the device itself cannot produce a page.

If the printer is not listed at all in the print window or in **Print Settings**, it has not been set up for this computer. See [Printing](../advisor-help/printer.md) rather than guessing at a driver or address.

## Ask Fin without mistaking the test fixture for hardware

Describe the printer by location and say what you already checked: **"Fin, the printer by reception did not print. I checked paper, power, and the selected printer. Tell me what you can see before making a change."**

If Fin refers to **Advisor Test Printer**, that is a built-in test fixture, not the printer in your office. It cannot prove that your actual printer is working. Ask Fin to explain the next safe step, or ask the person who manages the real printer or office network.

Do not give Fin document contents, a printer password, client names, or account information. The printer location and the symptom are enough.

## When to stop and get the right help

Stop if the printer asks for an unfamiliar password, a driver download, or an address you do not recognize. Do not install a Windows `.exe` or a random browser extension to force it to work.

If a physical error stays on the printer after you clear paper or close a cover, it may need the person who manages that hardware. The computer cannot repair a paper path, toner, or a network the office does not control.

title: Second monitor problems
markdown:
# Second monitor problems

Start with the connection. The external screen, cable, dock, or adapter can fail independently. Change one setting at a time.

## Check the screen and cable first

Make sure the external screen has power and is awake. Use its own buttons to choose the input that matches the cable, such as the HDMI or USB-C connection in use. If the screen says **No signal**, turn it on, disconnect the cable at both ends, reconnect it firmly, and wait a moment.

If a dock or adapter is involved, try one simple change: connect the screen directly if that is possible, or try a known-good cable. Do not replace several parts at once. That makes it hard to tell whether the cable, adapter, dock, monitor, or computer was the cause.

## See whether SP+ detects the screen

Open **System Settings** from Applications and search for **Display Configuration**. SP+ includes this display-settings tool. It can show the displays that the current desktop session detects, including the built-in screen when there is one.

If the external display is absent there after the physical checks, stop changing resolution or scaling. Note whether the monitor says it has no signal, the type of cable or adapter you used, and whether the computer's built-in screen still works. Then ask Fin for help with those facts.

## Arrange two detected screens

When both screens appear in Display Configuration, set up the simplest useful arrangement first. For two work screens, place the display representations so they match the physical left-and-right layout. Then move a window slowly toward the edge where the other screen should be. If it crosses over, the arrangement is right.

For a projector or a room display, you may want the same picture on both screens instead. Make that change only while you can see both displays. A separate extended workspace and a duplicated presentation are different choices, so do not assume the current setup is the one you need.

## Fix text that is too large, tiny, or blurry

Select the affected display in Display Configuration and make one adjustment. Resolution, scale, and rotation are display properties available to the desktop. Use the screen's normal recommended-looking resolution where possible before trying scale. If text is hard to read, change scale once, apply the change, and read a few lines before deciding whether another adjustment is needed.

If a change makes a screen blank, wait briefly rather than restarting immediately. Reconnect the screen that was working before the change if you need a visible desktop again. Do not keep applying unfamiliar display modes just to make the picture appear.

## When to ask Fin

Use a specific prompt: **"Fin, my external monitor is [not detected / showing no signal / showing the wrong picture]. I am using [cable, adapter, or dock]. My main screen [does / does not] still work."** This gives a starting point without sharing a client name, meeting content, or a screenshot of private work.

Do not install a driver, download a utility, or use a Windows `.exe` file because a monitor or adapter website suggests it. If the external screen is needed for a client meeting and the basic checks do not restore it, use the working screen or reschedule the display setup rather than experimenting during the meeting.

title: Something broke after an update: going back
markdown:
# Something broke after an update: going back

**Protect current work before trying to change the computer again.** SP+ can prepare an update in the background and finish it at a normal shutdown or restart. A problem afterward can be related to that update, but it does not prove the update caused it.

## Save current work

If the app still opens, save and close the work you can safely save. Do not keep editing a client document in an app that is crashing, freezing, or showing an error. Use another computer or a non-sensitive task while it is checked.

If the desktop will not open, do not repeatedly power the computer off and on. Write down what appears, when it started, and whether it appeared just after a restart. Do not send a screenshot that includes client information.

## Work out whether an update was involved

Record whether you saw a notice that a new SP+ version was ready and when you next restarted or shut down. Note the affected program or device, the exact non-sensitive message, and whether the same task worked before.

Do not treat a restart as proof by itself. A browser change, network problem, new device, or ordinary app issue can first become visible after restarting too. Those facts give an approved helper something to check instead of a guess.

## What going back means here

SP+ keeps complete system versions separately from your personal files. The current test virtual machine has the running version and one earlier system version. That earlier version may help when a technical diagnosis confirms that a system change caused the problem.

That is not yet a tested self-service recovery feature. This manual did not verify a rollback screen in Welcome or settings, perform a rollback, start the older version, or return to the newer one. A different computer might not have an earlier version available when it needs one.

## Do not make this a mid-work experiment

Do not use a terminal, boot menu, or online recovery guide to select an older version. Do not ask Fin to make that change while client work is open or a deadline is active. Changing versions can hide useful facts without fixing a browser setting, peripheral, or service outage.

Preserve the symptoms and use your practice's approved technology or support route. If none was given, ask the practice's technology or compliance owner. SP+ has no verified universal support or remote-assistance button.

## What a helper should check

Before anyone considers going back, they should confirm that an earlier system version exists, compare the timing with the update notice and restart, identify the affected part, and explain the expected result. They should also say what happens if the older version does not solve the issue.

If the issue concerns client records or blocks work, arrange a safe temporary way to work rather than making several untested changes. One controlled change is easier to diagnose than several guesses.

## Going back is not a file backup

Choosing an earlier system version does not restore a deleted, overwritten, or unsaved document. Your files are separate from the system version. Keep approved copies and backups of important work, and do not treat a rollback as document recovery.

title: The computer asks for a recovery key at startup
markdown:
# The computer asks for a recovery key at startup

**Stop and read the exact wording. Your files are not automatically gone.** A startup screen asking for an unlock secret means the encrypted storage has not unlocked yet, so it remains protected.

## Do not guess or share a secret

Do not keep trying an unknown key, and do not send a disk passphrase or recovery key to Fin, support, email, chat, or a caller. A legitimate support person can guide you without receiving it. Do not use a key sent unexpectedly by email or message.

Your normal sign-in password, a disk passphrase, and a recovery key are different kinds of secret. Do not assume they are interchangeable because a screen uses the word "password."

## Read the prompt before entering anything

Look for the exact term the computer uses, such as **passphrase**, **unlock**, **recovery key**, or **recovery code**. Write down the wording and any non-secret error message. Do not take or send a photo if it would capture a secret.

If the screen clearly asks for the disk passphrase you created during encrypted installation, enter that passphrase on the computer itself. It is not your ordinary desktop sign-in password. If it is accepted and the computer starts, make a note of what happened and ask support to investigate before changing firmware or startup settings.

## If it specifically asks for a recovery key

Do not assume every SP+ computer has a recovery key. The currently verified SP+ setup does not establish a separate recovery-key issuance or automatic-unlock workflow. The checked test system has LUKS2-encrypted storage with one unlock keyslot and no recovery token. It did not test a TPM, UEFI, real hardware, or a recovery-key screen.

Use a recovery key only if you were deliberately given one, recorded it away from the computer, and the setup record identifies this computer. If you cannot confirm those facts, stop and contact support rather than searching for a key that may never have been issued.

## What to tell support

Say: **"My computer stopped at a startup unlock prompt. It says [exact non-secret wording]. I [do / do not] have the disk passphrase I created, and I [do / do not] have a recovery key issued for this computer."** Also say what changed just before this, such as a firmware update, a new dock, or a BIOS setting change.

Do not include the secret itself, client information, or a screenshot containing either. Do not download a recovery tool, reset firmware security settings, or repeatedly restart the computer while guessing. Those actions can make a simple support check harder.

## What this prompt does and does not mean

The prompt by itself does not erase your files or prove that someone accessed them. It means the encrypted storage is still locked until a valid secret is entered. That is safer than starting with the storage exposed.

It also does not prove what caused the request. A startup, hardware, or encryption configuration problem needs a direct check. The recovery-key and TPM path remains untested for this manual, so support should confirm the actual setup before proposing a repair.
